passage:
Month one: Vinita got a big raise at her design firm in Mumbai. That weekend she bought a new phone, booked a fancy dinner and started taking cabs everywhere.

Month four: Her savings hadn't grown at all. Her brother Naveen asked, half joking, "Where does all your money go?" She checked her statements that night and felt a little sick. Most of it went to things she barely remembered buying.

Month eight: She had set up an automatic transfer to savings on payday, before she could spend it. She kept one treat a month, the dinner with friends she actually enjoyed, and went back to the metro on most days. When a colleague showed off a designer bag, Vinita felt a tug. She admired it, then let it go.

qa.q: What did Vinita start taking everywhere after her raise?
qa.a: She started taking cabs everywhere.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when she checked her statements?
qa.a: She felt a little sick and dismayed, realising most of her money went on things she barely remembered.

qa.q: What helped Vinita keep spending below her income growth?
qa.a: Automatically moving savings on payday, keeping one treat she valued and cutting habits she didn't care about.

qa.q: How might Naveen see his sister's changes?
qa.a: He might feel pleased that his half-joking question helped her take control of her money.

grounding: Shows a young woman noticing lifestyle inflation after a raise and changing her spending over months.

passage: Sarika, my child, sit with your Alka-aunty for a minute. When your uncle got his first big promotion, we moved to a bigger flat, bought a car on loan and started going to expensive weddings with expensive gifts. Everyone thought we were doing well. Inside, we were always worried about the next bill. One night I sat on the kitchen floor and cried over the car loan. Your uncle held my hand and said, 'Who are we doing this for?' It was a good question. We sold the car, moved somewhere smaller and gave simpler gifts. Some relatives gossiped. We slept better. Now you're earning well. Enjoy it, but ask yourself that question often.

qa.q: What did Alka and her husband buy on loan?
qa.a: They bought a car on loan.

qa.q: What does crying on the kitchen floor tell you about how Alka felt?
qa.a: It shows she was deeply stressed and worried, despite looking successful to others.

qa.q: What question does Alka want Sarika to keep asking?
qa.a: 'Who are we doing this for?' — so Sarika can separate real needs from spending to impress others.

qa.q: How did relatives see the couple's simpler life?
qa.a: Some gossiped, probably thinking the couple had fallen on hard times.

grounding: Shows an elder sharing how spending for image caused stress and how simpler choices helped.

passage: Bidisha had just been promoted at her bank in Kolkata, and three weddings were coming up in one month. Her cousin Bhupen called. "Everyone's wearing designer outfits this season. You'll look poor if you don't." Bidisha felt a knot in her stomach. Her mother's medical bills had just come in, and her savings were thin. She opened her wardrobe and found two silk saris she'd barely worn. She decided to borrow a necklace from her aunt and spend only on thoughtful gifts. At the first wedding, a cousin whispered about her 'old sari'. Bidisha's face flushed. But at the end of the month, the medical bills were paid on time, and she felt steady instead of anxious.

qa.q: How many weddings were coming up in one month?
qa.a: Three weddings were coming up.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling when Bhupen talked about designer outfits?
qa.a: She felt anxious, with a knot in her stomach, because she knew her savings were thin.

qa.q: What choices helped Bidisha separate needs from image?
qa.a: She reused her saris, borrowed a necklace and kept money for her mother's medical bills.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see her choices?
qa.a: Bhupen might think she looked poor, focusing on appearances rather than her real priorities.

grounding: Shows a young woman resisting pressure to spend for status when money is tight.

passage: Vidya's raise came through in April, and by May her colleague Raghav had plans for it. 'Now you can finally join the Saturday brunch group. And change that phone, it's embarrassing.' Vidya laughed, but at home in her rented room in Vadodara she looked at the phone. It worked fine. The cracked corner bothered her only when others were around. She made two columns on a sheet: what she needed, and what she wanted people to see. The phone went under 'see'. She decided the raise would first go to the savings she had been postponing and to her brother's coaching fees, and she would let herself spend a small, fixed part on fun, guilt-free. She joined brunch once a month instead of every week. Raghav teased her. Six months later, when his car loan instalments pinched, he asked how she managed. 'I decided before the money arrived,' she said.

qa.q: What did Raghav say Vidya should change?
qa.a: Her phone, which he called embarrassing.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel about her cracked phone?
qa.a: She felt self-conscious about it only when others were around, so the urge to replace it was about image rather than need.

qa.q: How did Vidya keep her spending below her income growth?
qa.a: She separated needs from image, decided in advance where the raise would go, and kept a small fixed amount for fun.

qa.q: Why might Raghav have asked Vidya how she managed?
qa.a: His own car loan instalments were pinching, so he began to see the value in her approach.

grounding: Shows a young woman resisting status spending after a raise by separating needs from image and planning ahead.

passage:
'Sahil, you booked a test drive for the SUV?'
'Just to look. Everyone in my team has one now.'
Keerthana put down her tea. 'Our hatchback is two years old. What's wrong with it?'
'Nothing. It's just... when we park at the office, it feels small.'
'Feels small to whom?'
He was quiet. 'To me, I guess. Next to theirs.'
'Okay. That's honest.' She pulled out her phone. 'Our rent went up, and we said we'd save for my master's next year. If we take a bigger loan now, which of those goes?'
'Neither, if we stretch.'
'And if one of us loses a job?'
Sahil sighed. 'Then we're stuck paying for a car that impresses people who don't pay our bills.'
She smiled. 'Your line, not mine.'
'Cancel the test drive?'
'Go and drive it for fun. Then come home.'

qa.q: How old is Keerthana and Sahil's hatchback?
qa.a: Two years old.

qa.q: What did Sahil admit about why he wanted the SUV?
qa.a: That the hatchback felt small to him next to his colleagues' cars, which shows the wish was about image.

qa.q: How did Keerthana help Sahil separate need from image?
qa.a: She asked whose feeling it was and linked the choice to their real goals, the higher rent and her master's, and to the risk of a job loss.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel when Sahil comes up with the line about impressing people?
qa.a: Pleased and relieved, since he reached the conclusion himself instead of being lectured 😊

grounding: A couple's conversation shows separating needs from image and avoiding lifestyle inflation in a car purchase.

passage: When I, Trisha, got my first big raise last year, I didn't notice my spending grow. It just did. A flat with a balcony because "I deserved it". A new phone because my old one looked embarrassing in meetings. Weekend brunches at the café where everyone from work went. Six months later my salary was forty percent higher and my savings were exactly where they had been. My friend Parul, who earns less than me, had quietly saved for a trip to Ladakh. I asked how. She said, "I only upgrade when something is broken or making me miserable. Not when someone at work has a nicer one." That stayed with me. I went through my spending and marked each item: need, want, or image. The image column was long. I kept the balcony flat, because I truly love it. I stopped the brunches I only went to so I'd be seen.

qa.q: How much higher was Trisha's salary after six months?
qa.a: Forty percent higher.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling on comparing savings with Parul?
qa.a: Trisha felt surprised and a little embarrassed that a friend earning less had saved more.

qa.q: How did sorting spending into need, want and image help?
qa.a: It separated real value, like the balcony, from spending for appearances, like brunches to be seen, so Trisha could cut the right things.

qa.q: How might Parul feel about Trisha asking?
qa.a: Parul probably felt pleased to share, and quietly glad her simple habit helped a friend.

grounding: A young professional looks back on lifestyle creep after a raise and learns to separate needs from image.

passage: Employee wellbeing counsellor's note. Jasleen (sales) came in saying she felt "always broke" despite two raises in eighteen months. She wasn't in crisis, just stressed. We looked at her month together, without judgement. Rent had doubled after she moved closer to her team's favourite neighbourhood; three subscriptions she had forgotten; a car loan taken soon after her colleague Vidya bought a car. She said, "I didn't even want the car. I just didn't want to be the only one on the metro." That was the real moment. She decided, not me, to keep the flat, cancel the subscriptions, and think about selling the car. She also asked for the company's list of registered financial advisers. I suggested she talk to Vidya honestly; she laughed and said Vidya had admitted the same thing. We meet again in a month.

qa.q: How many raises had Jasleen had in eighteen months?
qa.a: Two raises.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling when she said she didn't even want the car?
qa.a: Jasleen felt a mix of relief and embarrassment, admitting she bought it to avoid feeling left out.

qa.q: What made the counsellor's approach helpful?
qa.a: Looking at the month without judgement, letting Jasleen make the decisions, and pointing her to registered advisers.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel about Jasleen's honesty?
qa.a: Vidya seems to have felt the same pressure, so hearing Jasleen admit it may bring relief and shared understanding.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young employee realising her rising costs came from status spending, not needs.

passage:
Saturday
Mohit's wedding plans arrived in the group chat today: a bachelor trip to Goa, matching sherwanis for all six of us, and a cocktail night at a hotel. My share would be more than two months' rent. Everyone replied with fire emojis. I stared at my phone for an hour.
I love Mohit. I've known him since Class 3. But I've just finished paying off my laptop, and I'm saving to move out of my uncle's house.
So I called him instead of typing. I said, "Bro, I'm coming to everything that matters. I can't do Goa or the matching sherwani. I'll wear my best suit and be there from haldi to vidaai." He went quiet, then said, "Honestly, half the group can't afford Goa either. They're too scared to say."
Maybe I'll suggest a day trip to Lonavala instead. I felt lighter after that call than after my last raise.
— Francis

qa.q: How many friends were to wear matching sherwanis?
qa.a: All six.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling while staring at the phone for an hour?
qa.a: Francis felt torn and stressed, loving Mohit but worried about the cost.

qa.q: What made Francis's call a good way to handle the pressure?
qa.a: Francis spoke directly, said what was possible, committed to what mattered, and the honesty revealed that others felt the same.

qa.q: How does Mohit react to Francis's call?
qa.a: Mohit goes quiet, then admits half the group can't afford it either, suggesting relief that someone finally said it.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult declining costly wedding extras while staying close to a friend.

passage:

passage:
The junior engineer's quarters in the district town of Hingoli had a small porch and a scooter parked on it. Siddharth had been posted there for a year, and the scooter did everything he needed.

Then his cousin's wedding came. At the reception, relatives asked, "Still on a scooter? A government engineer?" One uncle said a big SUV would bring better marriage proposals.

On the drive home in a borrowed car, Siddharth felt small, then irritated at himself for feeling small.

He called his friend Hrithik from college. "Tell me honestly. Am I being stingy?"

Hrithik laughed. "Do you need a car for work?"

"The department gives me a jeep for site visits."

"Then you need a car for the wedding season. That's not a need, that's a costume."

Siddharth laughed too. He kept the scooter. When his pay went up that April, he left the extra in savings and bought his mother the reading glasses she had been putting off.

qa.q: What does the department give Siddharth for site visits?
qa.a: The department gives him a jeep for site visits.

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel on the drive home from the reception?
qa.a: Siddharth felt small and embarrassed by the relatives' comments, then irritated with himself for caring.

qa.q: How did Hrithik help Siddharth separate need from image?
qa.a: He asked whether a car was needed for work, and when it wasn't, pointed out the car would only be for show.

qa.q: How might the relatives see Siddharth's choice to keep the scooter?
qa.a: Some relatives may still think it looks odd for a government engineer, as they judge by status rather than by what he needs.

grounding: A young engineer in a small town resists pressure to buy a status car and keeps spending on needs, not image.

passage:
After her promotion in Seoul, Soo-ah noticed the bags. Every woman in the new team carried one of three famous designer handbags. Hers was canvas, from a street market in her university days.

At dinner, she said to Wei, "I think I should buy one. It's like a uniform."

Wei, cutting kimchi pancake, asked, "Did anyone say anything?"

"No. But I feel them looking."

"Or you feel yourself looking."

She was quiet. It was true that no one had mentioned it.

That weekend she walked through the department store and stood in front of the bags for a long time. The price was more than her raise for three months. She thought about the trip to visit her grandmother in Busan that she kept postponing.

She walked out without one, a little sad and a little proud. On Monday, she carried the canvas bag. At lunch, a senior colleague asked where she had got it. "My university market," she said. "Ten years ago."

qa.q: What kind of bag did Soo-ah carry?
qa.a: Her bag was canvas, from a street market in her university days.

qa.q: How did Soo-ah feel walking out of the department store?
qa.a: Soo-ah felt a little sad and a little proud, having chosen what she valued over fitting in.

qa.q: What helped Soo-ah decide against the bag?
qa.a: Checking whether anyone had actually commented and comparing the price with the trip to visit her grandmother helped her separate image from needs.

qa.q: How does Wei see Soo-ah's worry about the bags?
qa.a: Wei gently suggests the pressure may come from her own feelings more than from colleagues, helping her see it clearly.

grounding: After a promotion abroad, a young woman resists a status purchase by separating image from what she truly values.

passage:
At the tech company's Gurugram office, the lunch table talk was always about upgrades: new phones, new cars, weekend trips. Devika had just got a raise. Her colleague Yamini said, "Now you can finally get a decent car. Everyone judges the one you park."
Devika felt the pull. Her old hatchback looked shabby next to the new SUVs in the basement.
That evening she sat with her notebook. Her rent had gone up. She was helping her brother with college. She had wanted to build savings to take a course abroad someday.
She asked herself: would a new car make her life better, or just make her look better at the lunch table?
She kept the hatchback and got it serviced and cleaned. She did book one weekend trip with friends, which she'd been dreaming of. At lunch, when Yamini asked, Devika said, "Car's fine. I'm saving for something bigger." Nobody cared as much as she'd feared.

qa.q: What did Yamini say Devika could finally get?
qa.a: A decent car.

qa.q: How did Devika feel about her old hatchback in the office basement?
qa.a: Devika felt self-conscious and tempted, as it looked shabby next to the new SUVs.

qa.q: Which question helped Devika separate needs from image?
qa.a: Whether a new car would make her life better or just make her look better, which helped her choose her own priorities.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Devika's answer at lunch?
qa.a: Yamini probably didn't think much of it, showing that the judgement Devika feared was smaller than expected.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional resisting status spending after a raise and aligning expenses with her priorities.

passage:
Hi Bhupen,
You asked how I avoided "going crazy" after the raise. Honestly, I almost did.
The week the raise came through, I nearly signed up for a bigger flat, a gym membership that costs more than my old rent, and a new phone. I'd scrolled through colleagues' posts and felt behind.
Then I remembered my father, who got a promotion when I was ten and moved us to a nicer house, and then was stressed about bills for years.
So I made a rule for myself, which I'm not saying anyone else should follow: when income goes up, I first decide what I'm saving toward, then allow one thing that really improves my life. I chose a better mattress because I sleep badly.
The flat can wait. The phone works. I feel calmer than I did with the fancy stuff in my cart.
Nandini

qa.q: What did Nandini choose as the one thing that improves life?
qa.a: A better mattress.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel after scrolling through colleagues' posts?
qa.a: Nandini felt behind and tempted to spend on a bigger flat, gym and phone.

qa.q: What memory helped Nandini avoid lifestyle inflation, and why?
qa.a: Remembering Nandini's father's stress after upgrading their house showed that raising spending with income can bring worry, not comfort.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Nandini's approach?
qa.a: Bhupen might find it sensible and calming, and think about Bhupen's own spending.

grounding: Shows a young professional avoiding lifestyle inflation after a raise by separating real needs from image.

passage:
Sarika, you asked on the show about my wedding. I'm Nitin, and here's the story.
Everyone in my family expected a big wedding: three functions, five hundred guests, the works. My fiancée and I had good jobs, so relatives assumed we'd "show it". Some suggested a loan.
We sat down one night and listed what mattered to us: our families, a few close friends, good food, and starting married life without debt. The big wedding didn't fit most of that.
Telling my parents was hard. My mother cried and said people would think we were struggling. I said, "Let them. We're not."
We had one function, a hundred and fifty guests, a lovely lunch. Some relatives grumbled. But no one remembers the size now. What I remember is my grandmother dancing.
We used what we'd saved for a small home deposit instead.

qa.q: How many guests came to Nitin's wedding?
qa.a: A hundred and fifty guests.

qa.q: How did Nitin's mother feel about the smaller wedding?
qa.a: Nitin's mother felt upset, crying, worried people would think the couple was struggling.

qa.q: What helped Nitin and the fiancée resist status spending?
qa.a: They listed what really mattered to them and saw a big, debt-funded wedding didn't match, then held firm kindly with family.

qa.q: How might the relatives who grumbled see it years later?
qa.a: They may barely remember the size, as Nitin says, while the couple still benefits from avoiding debt.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult choosing a smaller wedding to avoid status spending and debt despite family expectations.

passage: I'm Leela, Pallavi's younger sister, and I watched her first year of "real money" from the next room. After her promotion the changes came fast: a bigger flat in a nicer tower, weekend brunches with colleagues, a new phone every time one came out. She laughed when I teased her. But by December I'd hear her on the phone to Amma, quieter than usual, saying the salary somehow vanished by the twentieth. Then in January something shifted. She sold her second phone, which I didn't even know she had, and started cooking on Sundays. When her colleagues planned a pricey birthday dinner, she suggested a picnic instead, and half of them came. On the fridge she stuck a list with two columns: "need" and "looks good." I don't know exactly what she felt. She seemed lighter, though, and she stopped checking her account with her eyes half closed.

qa.q: What did Pallavi stick on the fridge?
qa.a: A list with two columns, need and looks good.

qa.q: What does Pallavi's quieter voice on the phone to Amma suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt worried and a little embarrassed that her bigger salary was running out by the twentieth.

qa.q: Which changes helped Pallavi keep spending below her income?
qa.a: Selling the extra phone, cooking on Sundays, suggesting cheaper plans with colleagues, and separating needs from image on a list 🙂

qa.q: How might Pallavi's colleagues see the picnic idea?
qa.a: Half of them came, so many probably felt relieved to have a cheaper, relaxed way to celebrate.

grounding: A sibling observes a young earner noticing lifestyle inflation and separating needs from image.
